item.title: Hikone Castle: A National Treasure Above Lake Biwa — Guide
item.description: Hikone Castle, completed in 1622 by the Ii clan — hereditary retainers of the Tokugawa — is one of just twelve castles in Japan to keep its original keep and one of only five designated National Treasures. The elegant three-storey tower, built partly from materials salvaged from defeated rivals' castles, crowns a hill of spiralling ramparts, plunging stone walls and trick gates above the eastern shore of Lake Biwa, and its foot holds the strolling garden of Genkyuen, whose ponds and teahouse borrow the keep itself as scenery.

item.title: Inuyama Castle: Japan's Oldest Original Keep — Guide
item.description: Inuyama Castle, completed in 1537 on a bluff above the broad Kiso River, holds what is generally considered Japan’s oldest surviving original castle keep, one of only a dozen that escaped demolition, fire and war — and one of just five designated National Treasures. Climbing its steep, creaking wooden stairs is a walk through unrestored history that ends on a top-floor balcony with sweeping views over the river to the mountains of Gifu, and each spring several hundred cherry trees ring the castle hill and the old town below, making the season’s festival the prettiest time to visit.

item.title: Matsumoto Castle: Japan's Oldest Five-Tiered Original Keep — Guide
item.description: Matsumoto Castle, nicknamed ‘Crow Castle’ for its striking black exterior, is one of Japan’s most important original castles and a designated National Treasure, its five-tiered keep dating to the late 16th century and standing as one of the oldest surviving original keeps in the country. Unlike hilltop castles, it sits on flat land surrounded by a wide moat that mirrors the black-and-white keep, and the scene is especially memorable when framed by cherry blossoms in late April or lit up during seasonal night illuminations reflecting on the still water.
